notes:
I've written notes for most verses. Two things limit what I found:

- **Few comments on single verses.** Most commentators deal with Exodus 37 as one block and send readers back to the original instructions in Exodus 25 and 30. Enduring Word's page on chapter 37 gives only the Bible text under headings that point to those chapters. Precept Austin's verse notes mostly say "see comments on Exodus 25." I didn't get to read those earlier chapters' commentaries. That's where the fuller material for vv. 3–5, 13–15, 18–21, 23 and 26–28 would be.
- **No real Protestant disagreements.** None of the sources I read show Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican teachers disagreeing on this chapter. I also found no notes from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Below I note only where I found a source's own church tradition.

---

**Whole chapter**

- Keil & Delitzsch list the chapter's sections and match each to the original instruction: the ark of the covenant (Exodus 37:1-9, as in Exodus 25:10-22); the table of shew-bread and its vessels (Exodus 37:10-16, as in Exodus 25:23-30); the candlestick (Exodus 37:17-24, as in Exodus 25:31-40), then the incense altar (as in Exodus 30:1-10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-1.htm
- **Why repeat Exodus 25?** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says the repetition isn't pointless. It shows that everything was made exactly to the "pattern shown on the mount," and that this match between command and result was essential to the purposes of the fabric. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-1.htm
- JFB also says each piece of furniture was made the hieroglyphic of a doctrine or a duty. The tabernacle was a "schoolmaster to Christ" and a "shadow of good things to come" (Hebrews 10:1). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-17.htm
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary gives a short key to the symbols: the incense stands for the saints' prayers; the lampstand for the Holy Spirit's teaching; and the showbread for what the gospel, ordinances and sacraments provide for those who hunger for righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-29.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes the order: first the furniture of the Most Holy Place, then that of the Holy Place. First, the mercy-seat, then the altar of incense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/exodus-37.html

**v. 1**

- **Why Bezalel is named.** The Pulpit Commentary notes that no other maker of the tabernacle items is named. So naming Bezalel here is emphatic. It marks the highest skill being spent on the most precious object. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-37.html
- Pulpit adds that Bezalel handed most other work to helpers but kept the ark, cherubim and mercy seat for himself. Since the ark never came back from Babylon, his masterwork is lost. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-37.html
- Gill (the page tags him as Baptist and Calvinist) disagrees with the Jewish idea that Bezalel built the ark alone. Other items are also credited to him only because he oversaw them. Gill cites Aben Ezra's view that the ark is singled out for the glory of the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-1.htm
- **Moses or Bezalel?** Deuteronomy 10:3 says Moses made the ark. Precept Austin says Moses had it made, but Bezalel did the skilled work. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-37-commentary Coffman calls the supposed contradiction only a pseudocon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/37-1.html
- **Practical sense.** The BibleHub study notes say Bezalel had already been called and filled with the Spirit for this task (Exodus 31:1-5). His obedience shows that a gift is meant to be used, not just admired. They also see the acacia wood as a fitting picture of God's lasting covenant presence. https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-1.htm
- **Size.** A cubit is about 18 inches, so the ark was about 45 by 27 by 27 inches, small enough to carry. The same notes say the ark points to Christ, the true meeting place of God and people. https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-1.htm

**v. 2**

- **Wood and gold.** The BibleHub notes link the gold covering on earthly wood to Christ's incarnation (John 1:14). https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-1.htm
- The Pulpit homily by J. Orr calls the ark "the meeting-place of righteousness and peace." It pictures a heart where God's law is set and on which the atonement rests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-37.html

**vv. 3–5**

- Precept Austin points readers back to its notes on Exodus 25:13-14. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-37-commentary
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the two poles were to stay in the rings at all times, even after the ark was placed in Solomon's temple. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01721a.htm

**v. 6**

- **The word "mercy seat."** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the Hebrew word *capporeth* means "covering." Because it was pure gold, not gold over wood, it was more than a lid. Since blood was sprinkled on it on the Day of Atonement, it concludes it covered not the ark but for the sins of the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/exodus-37.html
- A. W. Pink (on Reformed monergism.com) says "Propitiatory" is the better name, taken from the blood of propitiation sprinkled on it. The priests had no chair because their work was never finished. The one seat, the mercy seat, was kept for God himself. https://www.monergism.com/mercy-seat
- Pink also notes that the mercy seat hid the tablets of the law from view. In his words, There was blood between the law and its Administrator and His executors! https://www.monergism.com/mercy-seat
- William Kelly says the mercy seat covered the law that condemns human pride, yet kept that law in the place of highest honour, hidden from view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/37-1.html
- The BibleHub notes say the ark's modest height kept attention on the mercy seat above it, which points ahead to Christ's atoning work (Romans 3:25). https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-1.htm
- **Catholic reading.** The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the lid the "propitiatory." It notes the Hebrew means both "cover" and "that which makes propitious." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01721a.htm Thomas Aquinas says Christ was foreshadowed by the propitiatory, since he is "a propitiation for our sins" (1 John 2:2). The ark was like a footstool for the one seated on it. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2102.htm

**vv. 7–8**

- **Hammered work.** JFB says hammering a winged figure out of one solid piece of gold was something few, if any, craftsmen today could do. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Exd/Exd_037.cfm
- The Bible Says notes that the Hebrew word for "hammered work" is also used for the cherubim and the silver trumpets (Numbers 10:2). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v17-24.cfm
- Pink stresses that the cherubim were not fastened on. They were beaten out of the same piece of gold as the mercy seat. https://www.monergism.com/mercy-seat
- **What did they look like?** The Catholic Encyclopedia says it is impossible to be sure. Comparing Egyptian art, it suggests kneeling or standing winged figures. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01721a.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says there has been much debate. It lists guesses: guardianship (Herder), abounding life (Bähr), custodians (Gesenius). It concludes that a full picture of them must be for ever renounced. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/exodus-37.html
- **Images and the second commandment.** Aquinas takes up the objection that the second commandment forbade carved images. He answers that there was more than one cherub to show the many heavenly spirits, and so that the people would not worship them. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2102.htm

**v. 9**

- **Henry's reading.** He sees the ark, mercy seat and cherubim as a picture of a holy God, a sincere heart, and fellowship between them through a Mediator. God dwelling between the cherubim means angels attend him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_037.cfm Benson adds that their facing each other shows the angels' unity in service. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-1.htm
- **Looking at the mercy seat.** Pink says the cherubim did not look at the law that condemned sinners. They looked at what showed God's glory, Deity magnified by sacrifice. https://www.monergism.com/mercy-seat
- Clarke sees their bending, gazing posture behind 1 Peter 1:12: the angels marvel at the plan of redemption. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-peter-1.html
- **Catholic reading.** Aquinas reads the two cherubim facing each other as showing that heavenly spirits are at peace with one another (Job 25:2). https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2102.htm The Catholic Encyclopedia notes the Old Testament phrase that God "sitteth on [or rather, by] the cherubim." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01721a.htm

**v. 10**

- The BibleHub notes give the table's size as about 3 feet long, 1.5 feet wide and 2.25 feet high. They see the bread as God's provision and fellowship with his people. https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-10.htm
- Henry contrasts this bread, which was only to be looked at and later eaten by priests, with Christ's table, to which all Christians are invited. What the law gave but a sight of at a distance, the gospel gives the enjoyment of. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-10.htm
- Grant's Commentary (a typological reading) says the acacia wood pictures Christ's humanity and the gold his deity. The table speaks of Christ sustaining fellowship among his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-37.html

**v. 11**

- Kretzmann (Lutheran) sees the gold "crown" as heavy crosspieces joining the table's legs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/exodus-37.html

**v. 12**

- **The rim.** A handbreadth is about 3–4 inches. The BibleHub notes say the rim stopped the bread and dishes from slipping off. It also marked a boundary of holiness. https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-12.htm
- Kretzmann sees the border as a heavy moulding just under the tabletop, with a gold rim standing up above it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/exodus-37.html
- Grant says the rim kept the loaves in place, which pictures shutting out false fellowship while keeping the true. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-37.html

**vv. 13–15**

- Kretzmann places the rings beside the heavy moulding near the top, where the poles went through. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/exodus-37.html

**v. 16**

- Kretzmann identifies the vessels as plates for the bread, small incense vessels ("spoons"), and pitchers and cups for drink offerings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/exodus-37.html
- Precept Austin links to Exodus 25:30: the bread of the Presence was to be on the table at all times. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-37-commentary

**v. 17**

- **Solid gold.** Henry stresses that the lampstand was not wood covered in gold but all hammered gold. For him it pictures the light of God's revelation in the church, always fed with fresh oil from Christ (Zechariah 4). He sees the Bible as a golden lampstand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-17.htm
- **Why hammer it?** JFB asks why it was hammered when casting would have been easier. Its only answer is that it was done as ordered, for a reason not revealed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-17.htm
- **One piece.** The BibleHub notes link the seamless lampstand to Christ's seamless robe (John 19:23-24) and to unity. https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-17.htm
- The Bible Says notes that "menorah," the Hebrew word for lampstand, is still a symbol of Judaism and Israel. The lampstand stood opposite the table. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v17-24.cfm

**vv. 18–21**

- **Seven lamps.** The Bible Says counts a centre stem plus six branches, seven lamps in all. Seven often stands for completeness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v17-24.cfm
- **Almond blossoms.** The BibleHub notes say almonds bloom first in Israel, which suggests watchfulness (Jeremiah 1:11-12). They also recall Aaron's rod, which budded (Numbers 17:8). https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-17.htm
- **The ornaments.** Henry says some details, like the knobs and flowers, are ornaments we can't explain. We can still be sure they had a good purpose. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-17.htm JFB compares them to the flowers God put in nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-25.htm

**v. 22**

- The Bible Says stresses that the lampstand was not separate parts joined together. It was hammered from one piece of gold. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v17-24.cfm

**vv. 23–24**

- A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg). The lampstand's purpose was to light the priests' work, and it was tended morning and evening. The Bible Says links it to Christ the "light of the world" and to the churches pictured as lampstands in Revelation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v17-24.cfm

**v. 25**

- **Order changed.** Ellicott notes that the order of Exodus 25–30 is changed here, so the three Holy Place items come together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-25.htm Pulpit says the incense altar is now in its right place, unlike its position in Exodus 30. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-25.htm
- **The horns.** The BibleHub notes say horns stand for strength and refuge; people fleeing danger grasped them (1 Kings 1:50-51). Once a year blood was put on them (Exodus 30:10). This shows that even at the altar of prayer, sinners come near only through atonement. https://biblehub.com/exodus/37-25.htm

**v. 26**

- Henry says the burned incense pictured both the saints' prayers and Christ's intercession, which makes those prayers acceptable. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_037.cfm
- **Gold, not bronze.** The Bible Says notes the altar's role is why it was covered in gold, not bronze like the altar of burnt offering. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v25-29.cfm
- **Where it stood.** The same page notes that Exodus places this altar before the veil. Hebrews 9:3-4 links it with the Most Holy Place. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/exo-37-v25-29.cfm

**vv. 27–28**

- Henry notes that even the rings and poles were gold, because they served in the Holy Place. For him our best service on earth is only brass next to the gold of the saints' service in heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_037.cfm

**v. 29**

- **Very brief.** Ellicott says Bezalel's mixing of the oil and incense is told here with the utmost brevity, pointing back to Exodus 30. The Cambridge Bible notes that the rules for their use are not repeated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-29.htm
- Pulpit compares Bezalel and Oholiab's blend of art and practical skill to Michelangelo and Cellini. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/37-29.htm
- Henry says God taught Bezalel the perfumer's craft too, though he hadn't known it before. Where God gives wisdom, he makes a person fit for every good work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_037.cfm
- **History of the recipe.** A BibleHub article says no ancient record outside the Bible confirms the exact recipe. Josephus and rabbinic sources do confirm that a guarded incense mixture was central to Jewish worship. https://biblehub.com/q/is_the_incense_formula_in_exodus_historical.htm
